opus-5.5.text:
I think math is a really useful proxy, but it's a proxy. The nice thing about math is that it's verifiable. You can check whether the answer is right, which makes it great for training signal and for measuring progress. And a lot of what you need to do math well, like breaking a problem into steps, keeping track of what you know, noticing when you've made a mistake and backing up, is just reasoning, and reasoning transfers. So when a model gets better at math, it's usually getting better at something more general too.

That said, I don't want a model that's a brilliant mathematician and can't help you write an email or debug your code or understand what you actually meant when you asked a vague question. The goal is general intelligence, being useful across everything people care about. Benchmarks are a bit like the streetlight problem: we measure what's easy to measure, and math happens to be very easy to grade. There's a risk of over-optimizing for that and fooling yourself.

So my view is: use math, use code, use anything verifiable, because those domains let you push capability hard and the improvements tend to spill over. But keep checking whether the model is actually getting smarter in the messy, open-ended ways too. If the math scores go up and real users don't notice a difference, that tells you something. In the end the real benchmark is whether people find it useful.

r001.rationale: The response says math requires multi-step reasoning and that this reasoning transfers, making math a useful way to push capability and measure progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I mean, math is a nice thing to look at because it's easy to measure. You know when you've gotten the right answer, and it's kind of a pure test of whether the model can reason through a hard problem. So I understand why everybody gravitates to it. It's legible. You can put it in a chart and the chart goes up and to the right and everybody feels good.

But I'd say I don't actually care that much about math as a goal in itself. What I care about is whether the model is useful to people, and the vast majority of what people want from these things has nothing to do with proving theorems. They want to be understood, they want help with something messy and ambiguous, they want the model to be funny or kind or to notice what they actually meant instead of what they literally typed. Those things are much harder to measure, which is exactly why they get under-weighted. There's a sort of streetlight effect where the field optimizes for whatever it can see.

Now, I don't think math is useless as a signal. If a model gets dramatically better at hard reasoning, that tends to show up elsewhere too. It's a decent proxy for general capability, and the skills are correlated. But a proxy is a proxy. The moment you start training directly against it, you start teaching the model to be good at the benchmark rather than good at thinking, and you can end up with something that's a brilliant competition mathematician and kind of a bad conversationalist. That's not the tradeoff I want.

So my view is: look at the math numbers, don't be fooled by them. The real benchmark is whether people come back and talk to the thing again tomorrow. That's much noisier and much harder to put on a leaderboard, but it's the one that actually matters, and if you're serious about being great at everything you have to be willing to care about things you can't cleanly score.

r001.rationale: The response says math is a measurable test of whether a model can reason through a hard problem, explaining why people emphasize math benchmarks.

astra-6.text:
Math is useful because you can check the answer, and it’s a way to measure whether the model can do something that takes multiple steps. But it’s still a proxy. If you optimize too hard for a particular benchmark, you can get better at that benchmark without getting proportionally better at everything else.

What I’d like to see is the improvement carry over. Does the model write better code? Can it understand a complicated question and help you work through it? Math can be a good training ground for that, but being great at everything means you need a much broader view of what success looks like.

r001.rationale: The response says math can measure whether a model can handle tasks that take multiple steps, identifying multi-step reasoning as a reason to emphasize math benchmarks.

sol-6.1.text:
Math is nice because you can measure it. You can give the model a problem, check whether it got the right answer, and get a pretty clean signal. A lot of the things we actually want models to do are much harder to evaluate. Is this a good explanation? Is this useful advice? Those are fuzzier questions.

But the benchmark is a proxy. If you optimize too hard for one thing, you can get very good at that thing without getting better at everything else. What I’d like to see is that the techniques that improve math also improve the model’s ability to reason in other settings. Math is a useful place to develop those techniques, but ultimately you have to test whether the gains carry over.

r001.rationale: The response says math is measurable and useful for developing techniques that may transfer to reasoning elsewhere, but does not identify encouraging reasoning on difficult tasks as a reason to emphasize math benchmarks.
